weekly_ai_summary.policy_summary: MHRAは、小児予防接種の安全性を再確認し、予防接種が重篤な感染症から身を守るための効果的な手段であると強調しました。アメリカ大陸では麻疹症例が増加しており、PAHOは各国に予防接種と監視の強化を要請しています。

items.title_original: MHRA reaffirms the safety of childhood vaccination

items.article_text_original: Vaccination is one of the most effective and safest ways to protect against many serious infectious diseases Dr Alison Cave, Chief Safety Officer at the MHRA, said: “Multiple large, well-conducted studies involving millions of children worldwide have consistently demonstrated that there is no evidence that vaccines cause autism in children. “Vaccination remains one of the most effective and safest ways to protect against serious and potentially life-threatening diseases, supported by decades of scientific evidence in the UK and internationally. “The benefits of vaccination are endorsed by the NHS and all major UK public health and paediatric bodies as part of the recommended routine childhood vaccination schedule. “All vaccines approved for use in the UK undergo a rigorous assessment of their safety, quality and efficacy and once approved for use, we continuously monitor their safety through robust surveillance systems, real-world data, and international evidence. “We encourage parents to follow NHS guidance on vaccination and speak to a healthcare professional if they have any questions. “Patient safety is our top priority. We encourage anyone to report any suspected side effects to us via the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.” Notes to Editors: - Childhood vaccination is recommended by the NHS, the World Health Organization, and public health authorities globally as the most effective way to protect children from serious infectious diseases. - Before approval, all vaccines undergo robust independent assessment by the MHRA to ensure they meet strict standards of safety, quality, and efficacy. - The UK childhood vaccination schedule is informed by evidence-based recommendations from the Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation (JCVI) and supported by NHS clinical guidance. - Multiple large, well-conducted international studies, including national registry studies and sibling-controlled studies, have found no evidence that vaccines cause autism in children. - In 2.56 million US children, researchers found no association between MMR vaccination before age 2 and childhood autism. (Burstain, et al, Vaccine Reports (2026) - A major meta-analysis of data from over 1.26 million children in cohort studies and nearly 10,000 children in case-control studies found no association between vaccination and autism and autism spectrum disorder (Taylor, et al., Vaccine (2014) - Some vaccines contain substances called adjuvants that boost the body’s immune response to the vaccine. A commonly used vaccine adjuvant is aluminium, although this isn’t used in the MMR vaccine. A recent large-scale study did not find evidence to support an increased risk for neurodevelopmental disorders including autism, with early childhood exposure to aluminium containing vaccines. - The MHRA has published a vaccine safety patient factsheet to give patients and the public clear, accessible and evidence-based information about how vaccines work and how their safety is assured and a meningitis patient factsheet to help people understand meningitis, recognise its potentially urgent symptoms, and understand the role and safety of vaccination to help prevent it. - The MHRA conducts continuous safety surveillance through the Yellow Card scheme, analysis of large healthcare datasets, review of international safety data, and there is ongoing review by independent scientific experts. - Should new evidence indicate a change in vaccine safety, the MHRA will act promptly to update guidance and information for healthcare professionals and the public. - Parents and carers should continue to follow NHS vaccination guidance to protect children from preventable diseases such as measles, meningitis, and whooping cough. - Members of the public and healthcare professionals are encouraged to report any suspected side effect from medicines and vaccines through the MHRA’s Yellow Card scheme. - The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) is responsible for regulating all medicines and medical devices in the UK by ensuring they work and are acceptably safe. All work is underpinned by robust and fact-based judgements to ensure that benefits justify any risks. - The MHRA is an executive agency of the Department of Health and Social Care. - For media enquiries, please contact newscentre@mhra.gov.uk or call 020 3080 7651.

items.article_text_original: The Region has recorded its highest number of confirmed measles cases in 22 years, while the public health risk associated with measles remains very high due to ongoing outbreaks, immunity gaps, and increased population mobility. Washington, D.C., 8 August 2026 (PAHO) – In a new Epidemiological Alert, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) called on countries across the Americas to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and rapid outbreak response measures amid rising measles cases across the Region. The call comes as measles transmission remains active in several countries and the Americas records its highest number of confirmed cases in more than two decades. As of epidemiological week 28 of 2026, ending on 18 July, countries and territories in the Americas had reported 47,459 confirmed measles cases. A total of 44 deaths have been reported in three countries. The number of cases is more than three times higher than the total reported during all of 2025, when 15,011 confirmed cases and 32 deaths were documented. Guatemala, Mexico, the United States and Peru account for 95% of confirmed cases reported so far this year. Although some of the Region's largest outbreaks have recently shown signs of slowing, transmission remains active in several countries. A public health risk assessment published this week by PAHO continues to classify the public health risk associated with measles in the Americas as very high. This classification is based on ongoing outbreaks, suboptimal vaccination coverage, the accumulation of susceptible individuals, and increased mobility linked to international travel and mass gatherings, factors that facilitate the importation and spread of the virus within and between countries. The assessment also highlights the increase in measles-related deaths reported in 2026 compared with 2025, the detection of cases in new geographic areas, and the disproportionate impact of outbreaks on populations facing barriers to healthcare, including Indigenous communities and groups with low vaccination coverage. "Measles leaves no room for complacency. We know how to stop it: achieving high vaccination coverage, detecting suspected cases early, and responding rapidly to interrupt chains of transmission," said Daniel Salas, Executive Manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. "Every outbreak exposes immunity gaps that must be urgently addressed, particularly among children, under-vaccinated communities, and populations with limited access to health services." Measles is one of the world's most contagious diseases. It spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The disease can cause fever, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis and rash, and may lead to serious complications including pneumonia, encephalitis, blindness and death. Vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent infection and stop transmission. According to PAHO's epidemiological alert, Guatemala has reported 30,371 confirmed cases and 26 deaths, the largest number of cases reported in the Region this year. It is followed by Mexico with 12,255 cases and 17 deaths, the United States with 2,260 cases, Peru with 1,277 cases, and Canada with 1,107 cases. The number of confirmed cases reported in 2026 is the highest recorded in the Americas since 2004, the highest level observed in the Region in the past 22 years. The regional situation reflects a broader global resurgence of the disease. According to World Health Organization (WHO) data, 186,168 measles cases had been reported worldwide by July 2026, representing a 12% increase compared with the same period in 2025. PAHO warned that young children not yet eligible for their first vaccine dose, unvaccinated or under-vaccinated individuals, Indigenous communities, migrants, displaced populations, and other groups facing barriers to healthcare remain at increased risk of severe disease and death. The Organization reiterated that achieving and maintaining at least 95% coverage with two doses of measles-containing vaccine is essential to interrupt transmission, protect vulnerable populations, and support efforts to restore the Region's measles elimination status. PAHO continues to provide technical cooperation to countries to strengthen surveillance, accelerate vaccination efforts, improve outbreak preparedness and response, and reinforce risk communication, particularly in areas with ongoing transmission and significant immunity gaps.
